rv.q: Allison Crutchfield’s recreations of their iconic suits, stylish but a little too tight, perfectly convey a duo in limbo: no longer schoolboys, not yet legends.
The production is entertaining and revealing.
The sincere acting, under Carol Dunne’s direction, and the acceptable accents override any lapses, particularly during the discussions of deceased mothers.

Because of that, and the fact that Crawford and Sears are so wonderfully charming, Only Yesterday is an enthralling experience that allows us to revel in our own memories of how much we, too, love the Beatles.

A warm soaking bath of nostalgia, Only Yesterday is sure to put a smile on the face and perhaps bring a teardrop to the eye of Beatles aficionados, especially for those of us who were young and self-absorbed back then and all our troubles seemed so far away.
Stevens’ play rises and falls on its own merits, which are just enough to make this slight entertainment enjoyable for even the most casual Beatles fan.

It’s thanks largely to the energy, facility and immense charm of these actors—and director Carol Dunne’s light, sure hand and obvious affection for the subject matter—that Stevens’s slight, often predictable account works as well as it does here.
Much like those bags filled with fan mail, Only Yesterday is jammed with words that are charming, funny, but ultimately pointless to the bigger issue at the core of these two young men.
If two Beatles sitting in a hotel room talking sounds boring to you, you're not wrong.

There’s really not much of a play in this 70-minute exercise, uninspiringly directed by Carol Dunne, whose chief interest is putting us in the private presence of Lennon and McCartney at the outset of their legendary careers.

'Only Yesterday' is Bob Stevens's first play. Prior work has focused on producing, writing, and consulting for television sitcoms. His lack of experience is evident here. It is difficult for Mr. Crawford and Mr. Sears to tackle this anemic script with any chance of overcoming its myriad deficiencies.

cn.t: Critics find this imagining of a night between Lennon and McCartney charmingly nostalgic with sensitive performances, though some fault the script for lacking new insights into the iconic duo. Reception ranges from warmly affectionate to disappointingly slight.
